We're a team that's passionate about astronomy and programming. Our skills include Python, data analysis, and scientific computing.

We've chosen the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge and are excited to explore NASA's astronomical data to build something innovative and inspiring.
summary:
Lost in the Spectrum is a free website that lets anyone explore how the infrared sky changes over time, using real NASA SPHEREx observations. Search for a star by name or coordinates, and the website retrieves its exposures from NASA’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). It subtracts the modelled zodiacal-light background, masks saturated and flagged pixels, aligns observations, and combines exposures from each visit into a single frame.

Visitors can step or blink between visits to investigate motion and variability, switch between six infrared detectors, or compare all six side by side. Every frame shows its real dates and data quality, with predicted positions and known asteroids marked. For beginners, the Featured section offers guided investigations: each opens a real example, such as Barnard’s Star moving across the sky, walks through what to look for step by step, explains the science, and suggests another star to try.

This answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by turning repeated, multi-wavelength observations into an interactive public tool. It lets students, educators and curious visitors explore the roughly 3,600 images SPHEREx takes daily without programming or archive expertise.

No AI or machine learning runs on the website; every frame is real, documented data.
details:
Lost in the Spectrum — Project Details

What it does and how it works

Lost in the Spectrum is a public website for exploring how the infrared sky changes over time using real observations from NASA's SPHEREx telescope.

Visitors can search for a star by name or enter astronomical coordinates. The website resolves the target using CDS SIMBAD and searches NASA's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) for available SPHEREx exposures covering that region, including the DR1 and QR3 data releases.

The processing pipeline:

  1. Retrieves the required image data from NASA's public cloud archive, using IRSA's cutout service as a fallback.
  2. Subtracts the modelled zodiacal-light background.
  3. Excludes unusable saturated and faulty flagged pixels, while retaining and marking pixels approaching saturation.
  4. Reprojects observations onto a common north-up grid.
  5. Combines exposures from each visit using inverse-variance weighting.
  6. Applies one shared brightness scaling across each sequence, so that the display itself does not create brightness differences between dates.

Visitors can step, blink, or compare observations side by side; switch between six SPHEREx detectors; combine detector images into false colour; or explore all six wavelength ranges in a linked grid. The website also displays predicted target positions, provides known asteroid overlays in the Every-exposure view, and offers a Details panel containing observation dates, data releases, exposure information, quality flags and source links.

Six guided investigations and an educational guide introduce beginners to real astronomical examples, including Barnard's Star and WISE 0855−0714.

Benefits and intended impact

Although SPHEREx data is publicly available, comparing astronomical observations typically requires familiarity with scientific archives, image processing and programming.

Lost in the Spectrum removes much of this technical barrier, making real astronomical data accessible to students, educators, researchers and curious visitors.

Its intended impact is to encourage more people to investigate moving and changing objects, develop scientific observation skills, and understand how astronomers interpret real data. It also provides educators with an interactive resource for introducing infrared astronomy and observational techniques in the classroom.

Tools, coding languages and software

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, reproject, Pillow and httpx.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite.
  • Astronomical data: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), SPHEREx DR1 and QR3.
  • Astronomical services: CDS SIMBAD and Sesame for object identification; NASA/JPL Small-Body Identification API for known asteroid positions.
  • Hosting and version control: Render and GitHub.

No dedicated astronomical hardware was required; the project uses publicly available space-telescope observations and computational processing.

How the project is creative

  • Time-based exploration: Instead of presenting a static astronomical image, the website makes repeated observations its central feature, allowing visitors to investigate changes over time.
  • Six-detector grid: Users can compare the same region across six infrared detector ranges simultaneously, with linked zoom and navigation.
  • False-colour imaging: Different infrared ranges can be combined into RGB channels to reveal differences that are not visible to the human eye.
  • Guided investigations: Real astronomical targets become interactive, step-by-step investigations rather than simply displaying scientific explanations.
  • Scientific transparency: The website preserves missing and unreliable measurements rather than inventing values, helping visitors understand the limitations of astronomical observations.

Factors considered

  • Scientific accuracy: Only real observations are displayed, with their actual dates, detector information, wavelengths and data releases. The website does not automatically claim that an observed difference is a discovery.
  • Data quality: Saturated and faulty pixels are handled explicitly, and warnings help prevent misleading comparisons between unsuitable observations.
  • Accessibility: Plain-language explanations, keyboard controls, adjustable blinking capped at three cycles per second, reduced-motion support and a responsive interface help accommodate different users.
  • Performance: Pre-built Featured investigations load instantly, while caching reduces waiting times for repeated searches.
  • Cost and reliability: The website runs on free hosting and tells visitors plainly when NASA's archive is unavailable.
  • Shareability: Every exploration can be shared through a URL that preserves its search and viewing settings.

Use of AI

No AI or machine learning runs on the website. All astronomical image processing, comparisons and calculations use conventional computational methods.

During development, our team defined the concept, selected the scientific features, established processing and data-quality requirements, directed implementation, and tested and reviewed the results. Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant to help write and debug Python and TypeScript code under our direction, as well as assist with editing and organizing project documentation and presentation materials.
